content.overview: BNS s. 34 — Things done in private defence.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence. The right is a shield against an offence, not against a lawful act of a public servant (subject to s. 37).
In student language: BNS s. 34 is the rule on “Things done in private defence”. The section provides that nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 34 exists so that “Things done in private defence” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
34. Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence

Essential ingredients
1. Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second, slightly harder hypothetical. Change one ingredient and show why the section then fails.

Layer 3 — Distinction. Contrast BNS s. 34 with BNS s. 35, BNS s. 38, BNS s. 41. Write a short table in prose: meaning, ingredients, stage of the case, consequence. Confusion of neighbouring sections is the most common reason arguments collapse under judicial scrutiny.



Layer 5 — Application and current-law close. Apply the test to the problem facts in IRAC form (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Close with: “The governing citation on or after 1 July 2024 is BNS s. 34.”

learningObjectives: Understand the foundational premise of private defence under BNS s. 34.
Analyze the defensive nature of the right: it is preventive, not retributive.
Identify the relationship of s. 34 with subsequent sections 35 to 44.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 34 provides that nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The right of private defence is a primary human right of self-preservation recognized by law. Where state machinery cannot immediately protect an individual from unlawful violence, the individual is legally justified in repelling force with necessary defensive force.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 34 (corresponding to IPC s. 96).
Pivotal gateway: Acts as the umbrella declaration for the entire private defence regime (ss. 34 to 44).
Nature of right: Purely defensive and preventive; never aggressive or punitive.
Burden of proof: Accused must establish circumstances of private defence on balance of probabilities under Section 105 BSA.
essentialIngredients: An act was committed which would otherwise constitute an offence.
The act was done in the bona fide exercise of the right of private defence of body or property.
The exercise conformed to the limitations set out in sections 35 through 44.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 34 is the opening declaration of the right of private defence in Indian penal law. It establishes unequivocally that an act done in legitimate self-defence is not merely excused, but completely justified: 'nothing is an offence'. The right exists because the State cannot place a police officer at every citizen's elbow. However, the right is subject to three cardinal rules: (1) it is a defensive right, not a right of vengeance; (2) it arises only against an unlawful aggression; and (3) it must be exercised within the proportionality and recourse limitations of s. 37.
examples: Teaching example (Repelling armed robber): An armed robber attacks a shopkeeper with a dagger. The shopkeeper strikes the robber with a wooden rod to disarm him. Section 34 completely protects the shopkeeper.

Teaching example (Retaliation after threat has ended): An assailant punches a person and runs away. Five minutes later, the victim chases the assailant, corners him, and beats him unconscious. Section 34 does not apply because the act was retributive revenge, not defence.
distinctions: Private defence vs Retaliation: Private defence repels an ongoing or imminent attack; retaliation punishes a past attack.
Private defence vs Free fight: In a sudden mutual fight with pre-agreed violence, neither party can plead private defence unless one party clearly retreats.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who inflicted blunt injuries on an intruder during a violent midnight break-in can claim exemption under BNS s. 34.
Rule: Section 34 provides that acts done in private defence are no offence, subject to statutory limits in ss. 35-44.
Application: Establish that an unlawful attack was underway, that defensive force was necessary to protect life/property, and that force used was proportionate to the threat.
Conclusion: If within lawful limits, the accused is acquitted under s. 34.

shortAnswer: Emphasize that private defence is preventive, not retributive.
Mention that it covers both body and property.
